summary: Specifies an RTP payload format and a file storage format for the AMR and AMR-WB speech codecs, designed to interoperate with existing transport formats on non-IP networks. It was replaced by RFC 4867.

eli5.summary: It is a way to pack compressed voice into network packets and store it in a file. It has been replaced by RFC 4867.

subtitle: Packaging compressed voice for internet real-time calls and storage

tldr.problem: AMR and AMR-WB are speech codecs that compress voice efficiently, but the RTP protocol needed a standard way to package them for transmission over IP networks and for file storage.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3267 defines how to format AMR and AMR-WB speech frames into RTP packets, with options for efficiency and robustness. It supports multiple frames per packet, error protection, and interleaving to survive packet loss.
tldr.outcome: VoIP systems and voice storage applications gained a standard format for these codecs. It was later updated by RFC 4867 to clarify and extend the specification.

today: RFC 3267 defined the original RTP payload format for AMR and AMR-WB and file storage. It was later updated by RFC 4867, which clarifies the specification and is the current standard.

sections.title: AMR and AMR-WB Speech Codecs
sections.content:
The Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) codecs are speech compression algorithms that squeeze voice signals into small amounts of data while keeping quality high. AMR was originally developed for GSM mobile phones and later adopted by 3GPP for third-generation cellular systems. AMR-WB is a wideband version of the same concept.

AMR supports 8 encoding modes from 4.75 kbps to 12.2 kbps and processes speech at 8000 Hz sampling, dividing it into 20 millisecond frames. AMR-WB supports 9 modes from 6.6 kbps to 23.85 kbps at 16000 Hz sampling, also using 20 ms frames. The word "Adaptive" is key: the encoder can switch between modes mid-call to balance quality and bandwidth based on network conditions.
sections.eli5: AMR and AMR-WB are special tricks for shrinking voice into tiny packages. They can switch between quick-and-small or slow-and-clear depending on how crowded the network is.

sections.title: Codec Features: Multi-rate, VAD and Silence
sections.content:
A key feature of both codecs is that the encoder can rapidly switch between different compression rates within the same call, responding to changing network conditions. This requires a Codec Mode Request (CMR) mechanism: the receiver tells the sender which encoding mode to use by including a request in packets it sends back.

Both codecs also support Voice Activity Detection (VAD) and Discontinuous Transmission (DTX). When the speaker falls silent, VAD detects it and DTX sends only short Silence Indicator (SID) frames with comfort noise parameters rather than full silence frames, reducing bandwidth use. This matters in VoIP where half the call is typically silence.

The payload format must carry multiple encoded speech frames (a "frame-block") in a single RTP packet, optionally from multiple channels (for example, a stereo or multi-channel call). Each packet contains a payload header with the codec mode request, a table of contents listing what frames are in the packet, and the speech data itself.
sections.eli5: The codecs can ask each other to talk faster or slower. They also stay quiet when nobody is speaking to save space. A single network packet can hold lots of compressed voice frames at once.

sections.title: Two Payload Format Modes
sections.content:
RFC 3267 defines two modes for packaging the data: bandwidth-efficient and octet-aligned.

In bandwidth-efficient mode, the payload header is just 4 bits holding the codec mode request. The table of contents entries are tightly packed: each entry is 6 bits (1 bit for continuation, 4 bits for frame type, 1 bit for quality indicator). This saves bytes at the expense of bit-level unpacking.

In octet-aligned mode, every field aligns to byte boundaries, making the payload easier to parse but using more space. This mode also enables optional robustness features like frame-level checksums (CRCs) and robust sorting of frames by sensitivity to errors. Between the two, only octet-aligned mode can use the frame CRCs and sophisticated interleaving for error protection.
sections.eli5: The format comes in two flavors: one tight and space-efficient, and one loose and easy to read. The easy one also lets you add extra checks to catch broken data.

sections.title: Surviving Packet Loss and Bit Errors
sections.content:
Over packet networks, frames can be lost or corrupted. RFC 3267 defines several techniques to survive this. The simplest is redundancy: a sender can intentionally send an earlier frame again in the current packet, so if the new frame is lost, the old one is still available. This works without any session setup; the receiver simply uses the highest-quality version if it receives duplicates.

For more sophisticated protection, the octet-aligned mode supports frame interleaving: instead of sending consecutive frames sequentially, frames are spread out so that a single lost packet does not lose consecutive speech samples. It also supports Unequal Error Protection (UEP): the most important speech bits are protected with checksums while less sensitive bits are not, saving bandwidth. This is inspired by mobile networks where some bits are more important to quality than others.

The RFC also mentions compatibility with external Forward Error Correction (FEC) schemes like RFC 2733, allowing the payload to be sorted by sensitivity so FEC can protect critical bits more heavily than others.
sections.eli5: If a packet gets lost, the sender can send the old one again. Or the format can scramble frames so one lost packet does not destroy one word. It can also focus protection on the most important bits.

sections.title: File Storage and Deployment
sections.content:
Beyond RTP, RFC 3267 also defines a file storage format for AMR and AMR-WB data in applications like email and cloud storage, with headers indicating single or multi-channel content. Both RTP and file formats come with MIME type registrations so applications and servers can identify AMR and AMR-WB data correctly. The RFC was designed to interoperate with existing non-IP transport formats for these codecs on GSM and 3GPP networks, so gateways could re-packetize frames between network types without loss of information.

RFC 3267 was later updated by RFC 4867, which refined the specification and remains the current standard for these codecs in RTP.
sections.eli5: You can also save this format to a file for email or cloud storage. The RFC also made sure that voice from cell phones could be passed to internet calls without mangling the data.
